Bots and webhooks

Last updated 17 October 2026

On this page
  • Webhooks
  • Outgoing webhooks
  • Built-in bots
  • Bots

Iskra has two ways to bring other programs into your server:

What it is Good for
Webhook A secret URL that posts messages into one channel Build results, alerts, game-server stats, anything that can send an HTTP request
Bot A program that joins like a person: it answers /commands, buttons and forms, and posts Dice, polls, reminders, games, role pickers

Both show a BOT badge, so everyone can tell them apart from people. Admins manage both in Server settings → Bots & webhooks. No programming needed? Turn on a built-in bot.

For server owners: Hosting reference → Bots and webhooks. How bots and webhooks are kept in check: How Iskra keeps you safe → Webhooks and bots. Where your server sends things: Who Iskra talks to.

Webhooks#

Make one#

  1. Open Bots & webhooks → Webhooks.
  2. Give it a name (and optionally a picture), pick the channel it posts in, and click Create webhook.
  3. Copy the URL. It's only shown once: the server keeps a hash of the secret, not the secret itself. Lost it? Click New URL (the old one stops working right away).

Treat the URL like a password: anyone who has it can post in that channel. Use the https:// address when your server has one.

Post a message#

shell
curl -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"content": "Build **passed** ✅"}' \
  https://chat.example.com/hooks/<id>/<secret>

The body uses the same fields as a Discord webhook, so tools that can post to Discord usually work by pasting the Iskra URL instead:

JSON
{
  "content": "Deploy finished",            // up to 4000 characters, formatting like chat
  "username": "Deploy bot",                // optional: a different name for this message
  "embeds": [{                             // optional: up to 10 cards
    "title": "v1.4.2 is live", "url": "https://example.com/changelog",
    "description": "3 fixes, 1 new map", "color": 5763719,
    "fields": [{ "name": "Region", "value": "EU", "inline": true }],
    "footer": { "text": "deploy #812" }, "timestamp": "2026-10-10T12:00:00Z"
  }],
  "allowed_mentions": { "parse": [] }      // optional: who may be pinged (see below)
}
  • ?wait=true answers with the posted message (JSON) instead of an empty 204.
  • Forms work too: curl -d "content=hello" <url>, or Discord's multipart payload_json.
  • Grafana and other tools with a "Discord" notification type: paste the Iskra URL as the Discord webhook URL.

GitHub, Gitea, GitLab and Slack#

Add a suffix to the URL and Iskra reads that service's own format. Events it doesn't post about are answered 204, so nothing retries.

Suffix Where to paste it What becomes a card
<url>/github Repository Settings → Webhooks → Payload URL, content type application/json Pushes, pull requests and issues (opened, closed, merged, reopened), comments, releases, finished workflow runs (failures, and successes of CI/Release/Deploy workflows), stars
<url>/gitea Repository Settings → Webhooks → Add webhook → Gitea The same as GitHub
<url>/gitlab Project Settings → Webhooks → URL Pushes, new tags, merge requests (opened, closed, merged, reopened), issues, comments, finished pipelines (failures, and successes that weren't scheduled). Confidential issues and comments are never posted.
<url>/slack Any tool with a "Slack incoming webhook" option text (Slack's *bold*, <url|label> links), blocks (headers, sections, context) and old-style attachments. Answers ok, like Slack.

Signing secret. Click Signing secret on the webhook, then Generate (or paste your own, 16–256 characters) and Save, and paste the same secret into GitHub's or Gitea's Secret field or GitLab's Secret token. Iskra then refuses /github, /gitea and /gitlab posts that aren't signed with it (401). A webhook with a signing secret is a GitHub, Gitea or GitLab webhook: its plain URL and /slack, which can't be signed, are refused too, so a leaked URL alone can't post anything. The secret is shown only while you set it. Webhooks without one keep working as before.

What's left out on purpose: images, thumbnails and avatar URLs from the payload. Showing them would make every viewer's app fetch a third-party address (revealing their IP). Give the webhook a picture in its settings instead.

Limits and safety#
Message text Same rules as chat (1–4000 characters, no invisible control characters)
Embeds Up to 10 per message, 6000 characters in total; titles 256, descriptions 4096, up to 25 fields
Request size 64 KB (1 MB for /github, /gitea, /gitlab, /slack)
Rate limit Per webhook: 5 messages at once, then one every 2 seconds. Too fast gets 429 with Retry-After.
Mentions Off by default: @everyone, @here and mentions of members are shown as plain text and ping nobody. Turn on Can mention people for a webhook you trust; the payload's allowed_mentions can then narrow it further.
Webhooks per channel 15

Nobody can edit a webhook's message; admins can delete it like any other.

Outgoing webhooks#

The other way round: your server POSTs to a web address when something happens, for things that don't want to hold a connection open (a Minecraft chat bridge, Home Assistant, IFTTT, a small script).

In Server settings → Bots & webhooks → Outgoing, pick a name, the https:// address, the events and (for messages and the other channel events) the channels. Events:

Event When
message.created, message.updated, message.deleted A message is posted, edited or deleted in a chosen channel (deleted: only its id)
reaction.added Someone reacts in a chosen channel
thread.created A thread or forum post starts in a chosen channel
voice.joined, voice.left Someone joins or leaves a chosen voice channel (who and where, nothing about audio)
member.joined, member.left Someone joins or leaves the server
member.updated A member's level, roles or server nickname change (never their profile)
role.created, role.updated, role.deleted Roles change
channel.created, channel.updated, channel.deleted Channels everyone can read (or that the webhook lists) change
event.started A scheduled event starts

Copy the signing secret shown once (New secret makes another). Send a test posts a ping, and Log shows the last 50 attempts (status only, never what was sent). Every member can see the webhook's host under My settings → Privacy & data → Who Iskra talks to.

Each request is JSON (the shape is in PROTOCOL.md):

JSON
{ "id": "3q2-7wAAAQ...", "type": "message.created", "timestamp": 1760000000000, "server": { "name": "Friends" },
  "data": { "message": { "id": 42, "channel": { "id": 1, "name": "general", "kind": "text", "parentId": null },
            "author": { "accountKey": "...", "name": "Alice", "bot": false }, "text": "hello", "createdAt": 1760000000000,
            "replyTo": null, "attachments": [] } } }

Check the signature#

Every request carries Iskra-Webhook-Id, Iskra-Webhook-Timestamp (Unix seconds) and Iskra-Webhook-Signature: v1=<hex>, the HMAC-SHA256 of iskra-webhook-v1\n<timestamp>\n<id>\n<raw body> (\n is a newline) keyed with the secret's UTF-8 bytes. Check it on the raw body (before parsing), compare in constant time, and refuse timestamps more than five minutes off. Retries keep the same id, so you can skip ids you've already handled.

JavaScript
// Node 18+
import { createHmac, timingSafeEqual } from 'node:crypto'

export function verify(secret, headers, rawBody) {
  const id = headers['iskra-webhook-id'], ts = headers['iskra-webhook-timestamp'], sig = headers['iskra-webhook-signature'] ?? ''
  if (!id || !ts || Math.abs(Date.now() / 1000 - Number(ts)) > 300) return false
  const expected = 'v1=' + createHmac('sha256', secret).update(`iskra-webhook-v1\n${ts}\n${id}\n${rawBody}`).digest('hex')
  return sig.length === expected.length && timingSafeEqual(Buffer.from(sig), Buffer.from(expected))
}
Python
# Python 3
import hashlib, hmac, time

def verify(secret: str, headers, raw_body: bytes) -> bool:
    msg_id, ts = headers.get("Iskra-Webhook-Id", ""), headers.get("Iskra-Webhook-Timestamp", "")
    if not msg_id or not ts.isdigit() or abs(time.time() - int(ts)) > 300:
        return False
    signed = f"iskra-webhook-v1\n{ts}\n{msg_id}\n".encode() + raw_body
    expected = "v1=" + hmac.new(secret.encode(), signed, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return hmac.compare_digest(headers.get("Iskra-Webhook-Signature", ""), expected)

Check: with the secret whs_test, timestamp 1760000000, id abc and the body {"type":"ping"}, the signature is v1=61117e1080d5aed00a4e39e279580b31eabbedd00eda8331228b580fb2308c28 (the server tests check this vector).

Delivery and safety#
Addresses https:// only, and only public addresses: the server checks the address after looking up the name, on every connection, and never follows redirects. Private, loopback, link-local and cloud metadata addresses are refused.
Your own network For a receiver at home (Home Assistant on 192.168.x.x, something on the same PC or on Tailscale), the owner can tick Allow addresses on my own network for that webhook; plain http:// then works for those addresses only. Link-local and metadata addresses stay blocked.
Answer Any 2xx within 10 seconds. The body of your answer is ignored.
Retries 408, 429, 5xx, timeouts and network errors: again after 5 s, 30 s, 2 min and 10 min (with the same id). Other answers aren't retried. Order isn't guaranteed.
Turning off After 10 deliveries in a row that failed (after their retries), the webhook turns itself off and admins are told. Turn it on again in its settings.
Rate Per webhook: 30 events at once, then 5 a second, 100 waiting at most; more are skipped (and logged).
Never sent Anything from end-to-end encrypted channels, direct messages and group chats (the server can't read them), and messages posted by incoming webhooks.
Per server 10 outgoing webhooks
The secret The server keeps each signing secret to sign with, so it's in the server's database and its backups. Keep backups private, and make a New secret if one may have leaked.

Built-in bots#

Eleven small bots come with every server and run inside it, so there's nothing to install, host or keep running. An admin turns each one on in Server settings → Bots & webhooks → Bots:

Bot Command Does
Dice /roll 2d6+3, /roll d20 Rolls dice (up to 100 dice and 10 terms; /roll alone is 1d6).
Polls /poll Pizza or tacos? | Pizza | Tacos Starts a normal poll in a text channel (2–10 answers).
Reminders /remind me in 10m take the pizza out Reminds you about that message later (1 minute up to a year), like any reminder.
Starboard (react with ⭐) When a message gets enough stars (⭐ ×3 unless you pick another reaction or number; the author's own and bots' don't count), it gets a card in #starboard that links back to it. The card keeps its count and text up to date and goes when the message does. Messages from channels that are more private than the board never go there.
Birthdays /birthday set 14 March, /birthday list, /birthday remove Members who want to share their birthday (day and month, never the year; also in their profile for the server) get a greeting once a year, at the time and in the time zone you pick.
Welcome Greets people when they actually get in (after approval or agreeing to the rules, if you use those) with your own text ({name}, {server}, {memberCount}, markdown), optionally with a private welcome too. When lots of people join at once, they get one shared greeting.
Feeds Posts new posts from RSS or Atom feeds, new YouTube videos and, with the owner's own Twitch app, Twitch streams going live, each in the channel you pick, optionally mentioning a role. Only new things are posted (nothing old when you add a feed). The server fetches those sites itself (text only, never pictures), so it's off until you turn it on.
Tags /tag rules, /tag list Posts saved snippets (rules, links, answers to common questions; markdown, up to 2,000 characters). Admins and a role you pick add, change and remove them under its switch or with /tag set rules Be kind. and /tag remove rules; up to 200 per server. A tag can never ping anyone.
Suggestions /suggest Movie night on Fridays Turns an idea into a card in #suggestions (or the channel you pick) where everyone votes 👍 or 👎 (one vote each, changeable). Admins and a staff role mark it accepted, declined or implemented, with a reason if they like, and the author hears about it. A Suggest button card works too, and the /suggest message itself disappears. Optionally anonymous: cards don't show who wrote them, but staff can look it up (that's logged). Up to 3 suggestions per person every 10 minutes.
Giveaways /giveaway 1h 2w Steam key Staff (admins and a role you pick) start a giveaway with how long it runs and how many winners (add a role mention so only members with that role can enter). People press Enter; when the time is up the server draws the winners fairly and mentions them. /giveaway end, cancel and reroll (for a week after it ends). Bots and people who left never win, and a restart doesn't lose a giveaway.
Counting (count in #counting) Everyone counts up in one channel, one number each and never twice in a row (simple sums like 3+4 if you allow them). A mistake gets ❌ and the count starts over; the best streak shows on the bot's pinned card. Editing or deleting a number doesn't break the count. No points and no ranking of people.

Turned on, each is a bot member like any other: give it a role or channel overrides to choose where it answers. Starboard, Birthdays, Welcome, Feeds, Suggestions and Counting post in the channel you pick under their switch (they need to see it, not write in it); Tags and Giveaways answer where their command was typed. Each reads only its own commands (Counting also reads the messages in its channel), answers mistakes privately to the person who typed them, and stays out of encrypted channels. Turning it off removes it; turning it on again brings back the same member. Details: PROTOCOL.md → Built-in bots and Tags, Suggestions, Giveaways and Counting.

Bots#

A bot is an ordinary Iskra identity (its own account and device keys) that connects with the same protocol as the app and says it's a bot. The server remembers that, and:

  • shows it with a BOT badge,
  • only lets it in with a bot invite (made by an admin; single use), and never lets a bot invite be used by a person,
  • keeps it out of voice unless an admin allows it (Voice bots), out of group DMs and calls, and doesn't let it create invites, schedule messages or be made admin (guest, member or trusted only),
  • lets it send and receive direct messages, end-to-end encrypted like everyone's, within limits people control,
  • applies the same rate limits as everyone else (2 messages a second, bursts of 10).

What a bot can read is the admin's choice when making the bot invite (Can read all messages, off by default), and can be changed later in Bots & webhooks → Bots; everyone can see it (readsMessages on the member). By default a bot gets only:

  • its commands, button clicks and forms (interactions),
  • messages that mention it, reply to one of its messages, or start with one of its commands (/roll …),
  • its own messages.

It doesn't get the rest of the chat, and requests that read it (history, search, pins, threads, forum posts, docs) are refused with bot_no_read. Most bots never need more; turn it on for a bot that has to read along (a logger, a translator). Bots that joined before this choice existed keep reading everything until an admin changes it.

A bot can be given roles like anyone else, so a moderation bot can get Manage messages or Kick members. As for people, it can only act on members ranked below it, and a bot is never ranked above trusted.

Bots and webhooks stay out of end-to-end encrypted channels: a bot holds no channel keys and never counts as a reader there, so it can't read or post in them (the SDK skips their messages), and webhooks can't post into them. Commands still work there, privately: see Commands in encrypted channels. A bot can read and post in a voice channel's text chat like in any channel it can see.

Your first bot in 5 minutes#

You need Node.js 22 or newer, Git, and a server where you're an admin. Any server works, including one you run on your own computer. Prefer Python? See Python; any other language works through the bridge.

  1. Get the SDK. It lives in the Iskra repository, next to the app code it reuses (it's also packaged for npm as iskra-bots):

    shell
    git clone https://github.com/quikmn/iskra-voice.git
cd iskra-voice/bots
npm install

  2. Make a bot invite. In Iskra, open Bots & webhooks → Bots, choose Member as the bot's role (a guest usually can't post), leave Can read all messages off (this bot doesn't need it) and click Create bot invite. Copy the link. It works once, for 7 days.

  3. Write the bot. Save this as bots/my-bot.ts:

    TypeScript
    import { Bot } from './sdk/src/index'

const bot = new Bot({ name: 'Greeter', invite: process.env.ISKRA_INVITE })

bot.commands([
  { name: 'hello', description: 'Says hello', handler: ({ userName, reply }) => reply(`Hi ${userName}!`) },
  {
    name: 'score',
    description: 'Shows a score card',
    options: [{ name: 'team', description: 'Which team', type: 'string', required: true }],
    handler: ({ options, reply }) => reply({
      cards: [{ title: `Team ${options.team}`, color: 0x57f287, fields: [{ name: 'Points', value: '12', inline: true }] }],
      components: [{ type: 'row', items: [{ type: 'button', customId: 'cheer', label: 'Cheer 🎉' }] }],
    }),
  },
])

// Someone clicked the button: answer only them.
bot.onComponent('cheer', ({ userName, reply }) => reply(`${userName} cheers!`, { private: true }))

// Messages that mention the bot (it doesn't read the rest of the chat).
bot.on('message', (message) => {
  if (message.text.includes('pizza')) void message.react('🍕')
})

await bot.start()

  4. Start it with the invite link:

    shell
    node build.mjs my-bot.ts
ISKRA_INVITE='<the bot invite link>' node dist/my-bot.js

    In PowerShell: $env:ISKRA_INVITE='<the bot invite link>'; node dist/my-bot.js. It prints [Greeter] Online in "<server>" as Greeter (member).

  5. Try it. Type / in a channel: the app lists Greeter's commands. Pick /hello, or /score (it shows the <team> option as you type) and see the card; click Cheer 🎉. /help lists every command (only you see that answer). Mention @Greeter with the word pizza and it reacts.

The bot saves its keys and the server's address in greeter.bot.json, so from now on node dist/my-bot.js is enough (no invite). Keep that file private: it is the bot. Run node build.mjs my-bot.ts again after each change. The build bundles the SDK, which reuses the Iskra app's own crypto and connection code.

The example bots#

Run it What it shows
Dice (examples/dice.ts) npm run dice /roll 2d6 (answers with a card and a Roll again button; /roll d20 yes answers only you), /coin, /pick pizza, tacos, /echo; commands with options; a button handler; reacting to "good bot" when mentioned; welcoming new members; answering in DMs
Music (examples/music.ts) npm run music A voice bot for the songs people upload: attach audio to a message that mentions @Music (or send it in a DM) and it joins your voice channel and plays it; /play <link to a file on this server>, a queue (/queue, /remove, /clear), /pause, /resume, /skip, /stop, /volume; a "Now playing" card with buttons; admins choose who controls it (/music-control)
Jukebox (gallery/jukebox) npm run jukebox A voice bot: /play [song] joins your voice channel and plays the files in a folder (and radio streams you list), /skip, /stop, /songs; a "Now playing" card with Pause, Skip and Stop buttons that it keeps up to date
Planner (examples/planner.ts) npm run planner /poll Pizza or tacos? | Pizza | Tacos (posts the result and a CSV file when it closes), /remind 10m stretch, /event 2h Game night, /events (a card); usage hints, edits, files, polls, events, an activity, and keeping state across restarts
Dice in Python (python/examples/dice.py) python examples/dice.py (in bots/python) The Dice bot with the Python SDK
Roll, any language (roll.py, Roll.cs) npm run bridge -- --name Roll -- python examples/bridge/roll.py A bot without any SDK, through the bridge

Start either one the first time with ISKRA_INVITE='<bot invite link>' npm run planner (PowerShell: $env:ISKRA_INVITE='<link>'; npm run planner). Each needs its own bot invite.

Gallery#

The bot gallery has ready-made bots to run as they are or copy and change. Each is a small folder with a README (what it does, its commands, settings and what it keeps), tests and its own package.json, so a copy works on its own with the SDK from npm (npm install, then npm start; Node runs the TypeScript directly).

Bot What it does
Trivia (gallery/trivia) /trivia start: questions with answer buttons (or answered by replying), points for the week and a results card every Monday. No levels, XP or all-time ranks. Your own question file works too.
Feeds Plus (gallery/feeds-advanced) Adds to the built-in Feeds bot: RSS, Atom and YouTube feeds with include and exclude keywords, and Twitch "went live" alerts in a channel or as a DM to each person who /twitch follows a streamer, with your own Twitch app. It only fetches addresses on the internet, never your own network.
Server stats (gallery/server-stats) A weekly card: members, new people, messages per channel. Counts only: never who wrote what. Needs Can read all messages for the full count.
Jukebox (gallery/jukebox) Your music folder and radio stations in a voice channel (see Voice bots).
Starter (gallery/starter) A template for your own bot: commands, a card with a button, tests and a GitHub Actions workflow. Also in Python.

From this repository, in bots/: ISKRA_INVITE='<bot invite link>' npm run trivia the first time, then npm run trivia (likewise feeds-advanced, server-stats, jukebox and starter). Their tests run with npm test.

Bots on this PC (desktop app)#

No Node.js needed: the desktop app runs gallery bots itself. In My settings → Bots on this PC, add one from the list (Starter, Trivia, Feeds Plus and Server stats come with the app and update with it), press Start, and either let the app make a bot invite on a server where you're an admin (with the rights that bot needs) or paste one. The app starts it with its own built-in Node.js, shows whether it's online, its last log lines and its settings (like the Twitch keys), and can start it with Iskra. Bots run while the app is open (also in the tray), connect out to their server like the app does, and nothing listens on a port.

Run a bot from a folder runs your own bot or a copy from the gallery: a folder with a package.json "main", a bot.js/bot.ts, or a bot.py (with the Python installed on your computer). Only run bots you trust: a bot runs with your rights on your computer and can read and change your files. A bot's keys and data stay in the app's folder for it (gallery bots) or in its own folder; the bot invite link is only used to join and never saved. Removing a gallery bot deletes its keys there; it stays a member of the server until an admin removes it.

The SDK#

API What it does
new Bot({ name, invite?, stateFile?, hearBots?, log? }) invite is only needed the first time. stateFile defaults to <name>.bot.json (lowercase, spaces become dashes). Bots ignore other bots and webhooks unless hearBots is true, so two bots can't chat forever.
bot.command(name, description, handler, { usage?, options?, role?, permission? }?) Answers /name. The handler gets { options, args, user, userName, channelId, dm, reply, defer, showModal, react, interaction, message?, command, bot } (see Commands); dm is true for a command typed in a DM. /help is built in and lists the descriptions.
bot.commands([{ name, description, usage?, options?, role?, permission?, handler }, ...]) Several commands at once. Every command is registered with the server when the bot connects, so the app suggests it when people type / and sends it straight to the bot.
reply(content, { private? }), defer(), showModal(modal) In command, button and form handlers: answer in public (a message that says who asked) or only to the asker; "thinking…" for slow work; show a form. Up to 5 answers per interaction, within 15 minutes.
bot.onComponent(customId or /pattern/, ctx => ...) A click on one of the bot's buttons or select menus: { customId, values, user, userName, messageId?, reply, update, defer, showModal }. update(content) replaces the message the button is on.
bot.onModalSubmit(customId or /pattern/, ctx => ...) A form the bot showed, filled in: { customId, fields, user, userName, reply, defer }.
bot.on('message', m => ...) Messages the bot may read (not its own): by default those that mention it, reply to it or start with one of its commands; every message it can see if an admin let it read all messages. m.text, m.author, m.authorName, m.channel, m.attachments, m.reply(text), m.react(emoji).
bot.on('dm', dm => ...) A direct message to the bot, decrypted: dm.text, dm.from, dm.authorName, dm.files, dm.reply(text). Commands typed in a DM also reach their handlers, with dm: true.
bot.sendDm(accountKey, text) or bot.sendDm(accountKey, { text?, cards? }), bot.downloadDmFile(file) Send a DM, end-to-end encrypted (cards become text); the bytes of a file someone attached to a DM (decrypted and checked).
bot.on('messageEdited' | 'messageDeleted' | 'reactions' | 'pollUpdated', ...) A message was edited or deleted; a message's reactions changed (the whole new list); someone voted or a poll closed.
bot.on('ready' | 'memberJoined' | 'event' | 'status', ...) Connected (again); someone joined; any raw server event; connection state.
bot.send(channelId, text, { replyTo?, attachments?, cards?, components? }) or bot.send(channelId, { text?, cards?, components?, attachments?, replyTo? }) Posts a message (up to 4000 characters; waits and retries if rate-limited), optionally with cards and buttons or a menu. A thread's id works as a channel id. reply(...) takes the same.
bot.edit(messageId, text) or bot.edit(messageId, { text?, cards?, components? }), bot.delete(messageId) Edit the bot's own message (cards and components replace the old ones, [] removes them); delete its own (or others', with Manage messages and a higher rank).
bot.react(messageId, emoji, on?) Add a reaction (on = false takes it away). Server emoji as <:name:id> (ids from emoji.list).
bot.sendFile(channelId, { name, data }, { text?, replyTo? }), bot.upload({ name, data }) Send a file (data is a string or bytes), or upload one to attach later with send(..., { attachments: [file.id] }).
bot.poll(channelId, question, answers, { multi?, durationMs? }) Start a poll; votes arrive as pollUpdated.
bot.thread(messageId, name) Start a thread from a message.
bot.setActivity(text | null) Show an activity under the bot's name.
bot.mention(accountKey) A mention token that shows as @Name and notifies them.
bot.channels, bot.members, bot.me, bot.channelByName(name) What the bot can see right now (kept up to date).
bot.joinVoice(channelId), bot.voice, bot.voiceChannelOf(accountKey) Join a voice channel to play audio (see Voice bots); the connection the bot has now, or null; the voice channel someone is in.
bot.fileUrl(file) The full address of a file on the server (an attachment), e.g. to play it.
bot.request(type, body) Any request in PROTOCOL.md, typed: events (event.create), pins (chat.pin), roles (member.roles.set), search and so on. Errors are RequestErrors with a code (forbidden, not_found, rate_limited, …).
bot.stop() Disconnects. The bot reconnects by itself after network trouble or a server restart until you stop it.

Commands#

A bot describes its commands; the SDK does it each time the bot connects (bot.commands.set in PROTOCOL.md). When someone types / at the start of a message, the app lists the commands of the bots that can answer in that channel: the bot, the command and its description. Arrow keys move, Tab or Enter complete, Esc closes. After the name it shows the options as hints (/roll <dice> [times]) and an option's choices to pick from.

Sending a command doesn't post it. The app checks the options and sends the command straight to the bot as an interaction; the server checks them again, and who may use the command where. The channel only shows the bot's answer, with "Viktor used /roll" above it. The rest of the channel never sees the command, and the bot doesn't need to read the chat to get it.

TypeScript
bot.commands([{
  name: 'roll',
  description: 'Rolls dice',                    // one line, up to 100 characters in the app (/help shows it all)
  options: [                                    // up to 25; required ones first
    { name: 'dice', description: 'Like 2d6', type: 'string', required: true },
    { name: 'times', description: 'How often', type: 'integer' },
    { name: 'secret', description: 'Only you see it', type: 'boolean' },
  ],
  role: 'member',                               // optional: the lowest level that may use it
  handler: async ({ options, userName, reply }) => {
    // options: { dice: '2d6', times: 3, secret: true }, checked by the server
    await reply(`${userName} asked for ${options.dice}`, { private: options.secret === true })
  },
}])
  • Options are typed: string (1–1000 characters, one line), integer, number, boolean (yes/no), user (an account key), channel (a channel id) and role (a role id). People type them in order, one word each; the last text option takes the rest of the line (/say #general hello there). With choices (up to 25) only those values are accepted, so leave choices out when any value should work and put examples in the description. args holds the text as typed, for bots that parse it themselves (or give a usage line instead of options: usage: 'Pizza or tacos? | Pizza | Tacos').
  • Who may use it: role (member, trusted or admin) and permission (like manageMessages) are enforced by the server, and the app doesn't list commands someone can't use. Which channels a bot answers in follows its own roles: it must be able to post there, so admins limit a bot with roles and channel permissions like anyone else.
  • Answers: reply(...) posts a message, or with { private: true } shows it only to the person who asked (never stored; they can dismiss it). Answer within about 3 seconds, or call defer() first: the app shows "Dice is thinking…" until you reply. An interaction takes up to 5 answers within 15 minutes; its token works only for this bot and this one interaction.
  • An offline bot can't be asked (the app says so). A handler that throws is logged on the bot's console (with the error code) and doesn't stop the bot.

Typing a command as plain text still works, for bots that don't take interactions and from older apps: a message /name args (or /name@BotName args to pick one bot) reaches the bot as a message, and the handler gets the same context with message set and empty options. Bots ignore commands they don't know, so several bots can share a channel. Limits: 50 commands per bot, names of 1–32 characters (a–z, 0–9, _, -), 16 KB for the whole list.

Commands in encrypted channels#

In an end-to-end encrypted channel the server can't read the messages and bots aren't in the channel's chain. Commands still work there, without leaking anything:

  • The app lists commands of bots that take interactions and can read the channel by their roles, and says before you send: "Commands go to the bot unencrypted, not through this channel. Only you will see the answer." The command and its options go to the bot like any request; the channel's messages and keys never do.
  • Every answer is private: shown only to you, never stored, so nothing unencrypted lands in the channel.

Direct messages#

People can message a bot, and a bot can message people, as end-to-end encrypted DMs. The bot has its own keys (in its .bot.json, with prekeys it rotates weekly like an app), so the server only passes the messages along, and whoever runs the bot reads them. The app says so at the top of a DM with a bot.

TypeScript
bot.on('dm', async (dm) => {
  if (dm.text === 'hi') await dm.reply(`Hi ${dm.authorName}!`)
  for (const file of dm.files) console.log(file.name, (await bot.downloadDmFile(file)).length, 'bytes')
})

await bot.sendDm(accountKey, 'Your turn in the game 🎲')   // e.g. bot.members, or the `user` of a command
  • Commands work in DMs. People type /roll 2d6 in a DM with the bot (the app suggests its commands there too); it stays end-to-end encrypted and reaches the same handler, with dm: true and the options read from the text. Answers are DMs: private makes no difference there, cards become text, and buttons, menus and forms are left out (they need a channel message). The bot checks a command's role itself, from the member list; commands that need a permission answer that they only work in a channel.
  • Who a bot can write to: members of its server who haven't blocked it. People choose in My settings → Privacy & data → DMs from bots (on by default). With it off, a bot can only answer someone who wrote to it first.
  • Limits: on top of the usual 2 messages a second, a bot sends at most 1 DM a second over all its connections (bursts of 30), and starts at most 20 new conversations at once, then 20 an hour. Bots never message other bots, and built-in bots don't take DMs (they run inside the server and have no keys).
  • People block a bot like anyone (its card → Block): then neither side can write to the other.

Buttons, menus and forms#

Bot messages (and private answers) can carry up to 5 rows of components: up to 5 buttons per row, or one select menu. A click goes to the bot as an interaction; the bot answers like a command, or updates the message.

TypeScript
await reply({
  text: 'Game night: who is in?',
  components: [
    { type: 'row', items: [
      { type: 'button', customId: 'rsvp:yes', label: "I'm in", style: 'success' },
      { type: 'button', customId: 'rsvp:no', label: "Can't", style: 'danger' },
      { type: 'button', label: 'Rules', style: 'link', url: 'https://example.com/rules' },
    ] },
    { type: 'row', items: [{ type: 'select', customId: 'game', placeholder: 'Pick a game', maxValues: 2, options: [
      { label: 'Catan', value: 'catan' }, { label: 'Codenames', value: 'codenames' }, { label: 'Uno', value: 'uno' },
    ] }] },
  ],
})

bot.onComponent(/^rsvp:/, ({ customId, userName, update }) => update(`${userName} said ${customId.slice(5)}`))
bot.onComponent('game', ({ values, reply }) => reply(`You picked ${values.join(' and ')}`, { private: true }))

// A form, shown to the person who used the command (or clicked).
bot.command('plan', 'Plans a game night', ({ showModal }) => showModal({
  customId: 'plan', title: 'Plan a game night',
  fields: [{ customId: 'title', label: 'Title', maxLength: 60 }, { customId: 'notes', label: 'Notes', style: 'paragraph', required: false }],
}))
bot.onModalSubmit('plan', ({ fields, reply }) => reply(`📅 ${fields.title} is planned`))
Limits
Rows Up to 5; a row has 1–5 buttons or one select menu
customId 1–100 printable ASCII characters, unique in the message
Buttons label 1–80 characters; style primary, secondary (default), success, danger or link. A link button has a url (http/https) instead of a customId: the app shows the address and opens it only when clicked, and the bot never hears of it
Select menus 1–25 options (label, value, description?, default?); minValues 0–25 and maxValues 1–25 (default 1)
Forms A title (up to 45 characters) and 1–5 fields (short: one line, up to 1000 characters, default 200; paragraph: up to 4000); each form can be sent once
All components 8 KB per message

Only bots can add components, and only to their own messages. The server checks every click before the bot hears of it: the button must really be on the message and enabled, and picked values must be the menu's own.

Cards#

Bots can attach cards to their messages, in the same format and with the same limits as webhook embeds: a title (with a link), a description, fields, a colour, an author, a footer and a time.

TypeScript
await message.reply({
  text: 'Your roll',                            // optional when there are cards
  cards: [{
    title: '🎲 2d6', description: '**7**', color: 0x695bff,
    fields: [{ name: 'Dice', value: '3, 4', inline: true }],
    thumbnail: { url: picture.url },            // a file the bot uploaded: const picture = await bot.upload({ name, data })
    footer: { text: 'Good luck' },
  }],
})

Unlike webhooks, cards can have a thumbnail and an image, but only from the server itself: a file the bot uploaded (bot.upload, then use its url) or a small data:image/png|jpeg|gif|webp;base64,... URL (up to 16 KB). Addresses on other sites are refused, so nobody's app ever loads something from a third party. Only bots can send cards.

Voice bots#

A bot can join a voice channel and play audio into it: music from files, sounds, or a radio stream. An admin decides: tick Can join voice channels when making the bot invite, or turn Voice on for a bot in Bots & webhooks → Bots (off by default; everyone can see it, joinsVoice on the member). Then:

TypeScript
const voice = await bot.joinVoice(channelId)          // e.g. bot.voiceChannelOf(user): where the person who asked is
voice.on('trackEnd', ({ track, reason, error }) => console.log(track.title, reason))  // finished, stopped, replaced, error, left
await voice.play('music/song.mp3')                     // resolves when it ends
voice.play('https://radio.example.org/stream.mp3', { title: 'Lo-fi radio' })
voice.play(bot.fileUrl(message.attachments[0]))       // a file someone uploaded to the server
voice.pause(); voice.resume(); voice.setVolume(0.5)    // 0 to 2
voice.stop()                                           // stays in the channel
voice.on('kicked', () => console.log('a moderator disconnected me'))  // it doesn't rejoin by itself
await voice.leave()
What it plays A file path, an http(s):// address the bot fetches itself (a file or an internet radio stream), a server file (/files/… or bot.fileUrl(file)), bytes, or any stream of bytes. Formats: MP3, Ogg Opus, Ogg Vorbis, FLAC and WAV, recognized from their first bytes. AAC/M4A isn't supported (most internet radios also offer MP3). encodeWav(channels, rate) makes WAV bytes from samples the bot made itself.
How it sounds 48 kHz stereo, 96 kbps (128 kbps in hi-fi channels), with redundancy against packet loss. Other sample rates are resampled.
Where Voice channels it can post in (it needs that to be heard). Never stages, never end-to-end encrypted voice channels (it holds no keys). User limits, timeouts and server mutes apply as for people.
What it can't do Hear anyone: its voice token can't subscribe to other people's audio, and it can publish one audio track, no camera, screen or data.
For people The bot shows in the channel with the BOT badge. Anyone can mute it for themselves (right-click it → volume → Mute for me). Moderators can server-mute it and Disconnect from voice it (Move members), as for people.

Music (examples/music.ts) is the ready-made one: people attach songs to a message that mentions @Music, send them in a DM, or /play a link to a file already on the server; it joins their voice channel and plays them in turn. /queue, /remove 2, /clear, /pause, /resume, /skip, /stop, /volume 80 (0–200 %) and the card's buttons control it. By default everyone listening may; an admin picks who with /music-control (everyone, trusted and up, admins, or a role such as DJ), and people may always skip or remove their own songs. Its settings are kept in music.settings.json next to the bot. It also plays the operator's own files and streams from MUSIC_DIR, like Jukebox.

No YouTube, Spotify or other streaming services, by design. The SDK has no extractors for them and never will: taking audio out of those services breaks their terms of service and usually copyright, and it's what got popular Discord music bots shut down. Play files you have the right to play, and streams whose operators let you (many internet radios do). Only let people pick from what the bot's operator chose, or from files on the server: Music plays only uploads and links to this server's own files, Jukebox the files in its folder and the stations in its stations.json, never an address someone types (a bot that fetched any address it's given could be pointed at other computers on its owner's network).

Voice needs the packages in bots/ (npm install): @livekit/rtc-node (LiveKit's SDK for Node, native, prebuilt for Windows x64, macOS and Linux x64/arm64) and the WebAssembly decoders; see the third-party notices. The audio goes from the bot's computer straight to the server's voice service, like an app's.

What bots can't do (yet)#

  • Group DMs and calls: bots can't be in group DMs, call or be called.
  • Files in DMs: bots can read files people attach to a DM, but can't attach files to their own DMs yet.
  • Encrypted channels: bots can't read or post there; commands work, with private answers (see above).

When it won't start#

The bot says What to do
That doesn't look like an Iskra invite link. Copy the whole link from Bots & webhooks → Bots; it contains #/join/.
No server yet: start the bot once with a bot invite link … First start: set ISKRA_INVITE. Already ran it? You're in another folder, so it can't find its <name>.bot.json.
The server didn't accept this invite. A bot needs a bot invite … You used an invite for people, or a bot invite that was already used or expired. Make a new bot invite.
This bot is no longer a member of the server … An admin removed it. Make a new bot invite and start it with that (it keeps its keys).
forbidden errors in the log The bot's role can't do that there: check the channel's write level, or give the bot a role.
The server didn't take the command list (bad_request): … A command, option or choice breaks a limit; the message says which. Commands still work as text.
Its commands don't show up when typing / The bot must be able to read and post in that channel (in an encrypted channel: read it). Commands with a role or permission show only for people who have it.
forbidden with bot_no_read The bot was invited without Can read all messages, so it gets its commands and mentions only. An admin can change that in Bots & webhooks → Bots.
Nothing answers the button "…" in the log Add a bot.onComponent(...) for that customId (or a pattern that matches it).
forbidden with bot_no_voice An admin hasn't let the bot join voice: Bots & webhooks → Bots → Voice.
Voice needs @livekit/rtc-node: run "npm install" … As it says: voice uses packages the rest of the SDK doesn't (with the npm package they're optional dependencies; install them in your bot's folder).
forbidden with bot_dms_off from sendDm That person turned off DMs from bots; the bot can answer once they write to it.
rate_limited with bot_dm_new_limit The bot started 20 new conversations in a short time; it can start more later (answering people who wrote to it still works).
Couldn't read a DM from … in the log That message wasn't encrypted for this bot's keys (for example it was sent before the bot's .bot.json was replaced). New messages are.
Can't play AAC … / … is a web page, not an audio file or stream Use MP3, Ogg, FLAC or WAV; for a radio, use its direct stream address (often ending in .mp3), not its web page.
rate_limited The SDK already waits and retries sends; slow down loops that call bot.request directly.

The SDK on npm#

The SDK is on npm as iskra-bots (one ES module with the app's core bundled in, and its TypeScript types), for bots that live outside the repository:

shell
npm install iskra-bots
JavaScript
import { Bot } from 'iskra-bots'

Everything above works the same; the voice packages are optional dependencies. Each release is built and published by GitHub Actions with a provenance statement, so npm audit signatures can check it came from this repository. Maintainers build it with npm run build:sdk in bots/ (npm run pack:sdk lists what would be published); docs/ci-cd.md has the release steps.

Python#

The Python SDK (package iskra-bots, import iskra, in bots/python) does what the Node SDK does, except voice: commands with /help, buttons, menus, forms and cards, files, polls, threads, end-to-end encrypted DMs, reconnecting, and the same <name>.bot.json, so a bot can move between Node and Python and keep its identity. It's asyncio, typed, and needs only PyNaCl (libsodium) and websockets. Python 3.11 or newer.

shell
git clone https://github.com/quikmn/iskra-voice.git
pip install ./iskra-voice/bots/python
Python
import os
from iskra import Bot

bot = Bot("Greeter", invite=os.environ.get("ISKRA_INVITE"))

@bot.command("hello", "Says hello")
async def hello(ctx):
    await ctx.reply(f"Hi {ctx.user_name}!")

@bot.command("score", "Shows a score card", options=[{"name": "team", "description": "Which team", "type": "string", "required": True}])
async def score(ctx):
    await ctx.reply({
        "cards": [{"title": f"Team {ctx.options['team']}", "color": 0x57F287, "fields": [{"name": "Points", "value": "12", "inline": True}]}],
        "components": [{"type": "row", "items": [{"type": "button", "customId": "cheer", "label": "Cheer 🎉"}]}],
    })

@bot.on_component("cheer")
async def cheer(ctx):
    await ctx.reply(f"{ctx.user_name} cheers!", private=True)

@bot.on("message")                                # messages that mention the bot
async def pizza(message):
    if "pizza" in message.text:
        await message.react("🍕")

@bot.on("dm")                                     # end-to-end encrypted DMs; commands work there too
async def dm(dm):
    if not dm.text.startswith("/"):
        await dm.reply("Hi! Try /hello")

bot.run()                                         # until Ctrl+C; or: await bot.start() in your own asyncio code

Start it once with the invite (ISKRA_INVITE='<bot invite link>' python greeter.py; PowerShell: $env:ISKRA_INVITE='<link>'; python greeter.py); after that it finds the server in greeter.bot.json. The example Dice bot is bots/python/examples/dice.py.

Node Python
new Bot({ name, invite, stateFile, hearBots, log }) Bot(name, invite=None, *, state_file=None, hear_bots=False, log=None)
bot.command(name, description, handler, details), bot.commands([...]) the same, or @bot.command(name, description, options=..., usage=..., role=..., permission=...)
bot.onComponent(id or /re/, ...), bot.onModalSubmit(...) @bot.on_component("id" or re.compile(...)), @bot.on_modal_submit(...)
bot.on('message' | 'dm' | 'memberJoined' | 'messageEdited' | ...) @bot.on("message" | "dm" | "member_joined" | "message_edited" | ...) (the camelCase names work too)
Context: userName, channelId, options, args, reply, defer, showModal, update, customId, values, fields ctx.user_name, ctx.channel_id, ctx.options, ctx.args, await ctx.reply(content, private=True), ctx.defer(), ctx.show_modal(modal), ctx.update(...), ctx.custom_id, ctx.values, ctx.fields
m.text, m.authorName, m.reply(), m.react(); dm.from, dm.reply() m.text, m.author_name, m.data (the whole message), await m.reply(), await m.react(); dm.author, await dm.reply()
send, edit, delete, react, upload, sendFile, poll, thread, setActivity, sendDm, downloadDmFile, request send(channel_id, content, reply_to=, attachments=, cards=, components=), edit, delete, react, upload(name, data), send_file(channel_id, name, data, text=), poll(channel_id, question, answers, multi=, duration_ms=), thread, set_activity, send_dm, download_dm_file, request(type, body) (all async)
bot.channels, bot.members, bot.me, channelByName, mention, fileUrl bot.channels, bot.members (a dict), bot.me, channel_by_name, mention, file_url

Content is a string or a dict with the protocol's own field names (text, cards, components, attachments, replyTo); messages, members and channels arrive as plain dicts (typed TypedDicts). Failed requests raise RequestError with a code; a refused start raises Rejected (with the same explanations as in When it won't start). Handlers may be plain or async; one that raises is logged and the bot carries on.

The crypto is libsodium through PyNaCl, nothing hand-rolled, and its tests check it against the protocol's test vectors (protocol/vectors.json) and against DMs the app's own code encrypted. Voice bots are Node only for now.

Other languages#

Any language can run a bot through the bridge: a small program in the npm package that logs in as the bot with the Node SDK (the normal signed handshake, keys in <name>.bot.json) and talks to your program in JSON, one object per line, over your program's stdin and stdout. There's no HTTP API and nothing listens on a port: your program only reads and writes lines.

shell
# Starts your program and connects its stdin/stdout to the bot. The invite is only needed the first time.
npx iskra-bots bridge --name Roll --invite '<bot invite link>' -- python roll.py
npx iskra-bots bridge --name Roll -- dotnet run Roll.cs

Without a program after --, the bridge uses its own stdin and stdout instead, for a program that starts the bridge itself. Options: --name (or ISKRA_BOT_NAME), --invite (or ISKRA_INVITE), --state <file> (or ISKRA_BOT_STATE), --hear-bots, --raw. In the repository: npm run bridge -- --name Roll -- python roll.py in bots/. The program is started without a shell, so on Windows name its .exe (python, node, dotnet). The bridge's own messages go to stderr, and so does your program's stderr.

Two complete examples, each about 30 lines: roll.py (Python without the SDK) and Roll.cs (one C# file).

The line protocol (version 1)#

From the bridge (your stdin), events:

JSON
{"event":"hello","body":{"v":1,"bridge":"iskra-bots 0.2.0","name":"Roll"}}       // always the first line
{"event":"ready","body":{"me":Member,"channels":[Channel],"commands":[Command]}}  // online (again, after a reconnect)
{"event":"command","ref":"r1","body":{"command":"roll","args":"2d6","options":{"dice":"2d6"},
  "user":"<accountKey>","userName":"Viktor","channelId":1,"dm":false,"private":false,"messageId"?:42}}
{"event":"component","ref":"r2","body":{"customId":"again","values":[],"user":"...","userName":"...","channelId":1,"messageId"?:43,"responseId"?:"...","private":false}}
{"event":"modal","ref":"r3","body":{"customId":"plan","fields":{"title":"Game night"},"user":"...","userName":"...","channelId":1}}
{"event":"message","ref":"r4","body":{"message":Message,"authorName":"Viktor"}}  // messages the bot may read
{"event":"dm","ref":"r5","body":{"id":"...","from":"<accountKey>","authorName":"Viktor","text":"hi","sentAt":0,"files":[DmFile]}}
{"event":"memberJoined","body":{"member":Member}}
{"event":"messageEdited","body":{"message":Message}}   // also messageDeleted, reactions, pollUpdated (the server's bodies)
{"event":"status","body":{"state":"offline","retryInMs":2000}}                  // connecting, online, offline, restarting, rejected
{"event":"server","type":"chat.typing","body":{...}}   // every server event, only with --raw
{"event":"stopped","body":{"reason":"..."}}            // the bot couldn't start or was turned away; the bridge ends

Objects (Member, Message, ...) are the protocol's (PROTOCOL.md). A ref answers what it came with for 15 minutes (the last 1000 are kept).

To the bridge (your stdout), requests, each with your own id (a string of 1–64 characters, or an integer):

JSON
{"id":1,"type":"bridge.commands","body":{"commands":[{"name":"roll","description":"Rolls dice","options":[...]}]}}
{"id":2,"type":"bridge.reply","body":{"ref":"r1","text":"Rolled 7","cards"?:[...],"components"?:[...],"private"?:true}}
{"id":3,"type":"chat.history","body":{"channelId":1}}     // any request in PROTOCOL.md, sent as the bot

and the answer to each, on one line:

JSON
{"id":2,"ok":true,"body":{"message":Message}}
{"id":3,"ok":false,"error":{"code":"forbidden","message":"...","key"?:"bot_no_read","args"?:{}}}
Request Body Answer
bridge.commands commands: the command list, as above (name, description, usage?, options?, role?, permission?). Replaces the list set before; /help is built in. Works before the bot is online. { commands: [names] }
bridge.reply ref (a command, click, form, message or DM), and text?, cards?, components?, private? { message } (null for private answers and DMs)
bridge.defer ref (a command, click or form): "thinking…"
bridge.update ref (a click), and the new text?, cards?, components? of the message it was on
bridge.modal ref (a command or click), modal (a form)
bridge.react ref (a message, or a command typed as text), emoji
bridge.send channelId, text?, cards?, components?, replyTo?, attachments? (retries when rate limited; text over 4000 characters is cut) { message }
bridge.dm accountKey, text?, cards?: an end-to-end encrypted DM
bridge.upload name, data (base64) { file }, for attachments
bridge.dmFile file (from a dm event's files) { data } (base64, decrypted and checked)
bridge.info { me, channels, members, commands }
anything else the protocol request's body its result
Line length Up to 1 MiB per line from your program (longer lines are refused whole: too_large). Lines from the bridge have no limit of their own; they're as big as the server's events.
Encoding UTF-8, one JSON object per line, \n (or \r\n) at the end. Read stdin as UTF-8.
Waiting answers At most 64 requests at once (more: busy). Answers can come in any order: match them by id.
Before it's online Requests wait until the bot is online (bridge.commands and bridge.info don't).
Errors code is the server's (PROTOCOL.md → Errors) or the bridge's: bad_request (a malformed line or body; id is null when the line had no usable id), unknown_ref, unknown_type, too_large, busy, disconnected, failed.
Other output A line that doesn't start with { (a stray print) is passed to the bridge's log, not treated as a request.
Ending When your program exits, the bridge stops the bot and exits with your program's exit code; without --, it stops when its stdin closes.
Versions hello carries the protocol version (v: 1). New events, fields and request types can be added in version 1, so ignore what you don't know; anything incompatible would be version 2.

What the bridge doesn't change: the bot is still a bot (the same limits, read scope and badge), and the program it runs can do anything the bot can, so run programs you trust, and keep <name>.bot.json private.

Writing a client from scratch is possible too: a bot is any client that follows PROTOCOL.md: make an Ed25519 account key and device key, certify the device, connect to wss://<server>/ws, and send auth with profile: { name, bot: true } and the bot invite code (the last part of the invite link). The Python SDK is a complete example of that.
